newsitem.title: CHILE: U.S. salmon farmers give up Chile dumping claim.
newsitem.headline: U.S. salmon farmers give up Chile dumping claim.

text.p: U.S. salmon producers have decided on legal advice not to sue Chilean farmers for illegally dumping salmon in the American market, said Chile's Association of Salmon and Trout Producers on Wednesday.

"The U.S. producers consulted their own lawyers and they showed them they had no dumping case to present to the U.S. Commerce Department and so they decided against going ahead with the claim," said the association's general manager Rodrigo Infante.
The decision will defuse a potentially embarrassing trade row between the United States and Chile just weeks before Chilean President Eduardo Frei makes a four-day official visit to the U.S.
The United States is Chile's second-largest salmon market behind Japan, buying 30 percent of its output.
To prove dumping charges, the accuser must generally show the producer is selling below cost, or below the cost at which it sells its product in its home market.

In the early 1990s, U.S. salmon producers succeeded in anti-dumping charges against farmers in Norway, the world's largest salmon raiser. The U.S. government imposed compensatory tariffs on Norwegian salmon and Norwegian exports to the American market fell sharply as a result.

In the past 15 years, Chile has become a major producer of farmed salmon. Output has gone from virtually zero in the late 1970s to about 100,000 tonnes in 1995, making it the world's second largest producer of farmed salmon.
Local salmon raisers admit Chile's booming production has contributed to a sharp drop in supermarket salmon prices around the world.
